Let $Q=(Q_0,Q_1,s,t)$ be a finite quiver: $Q_0$ and $Q_1$ are finite sets,
and $s,t:Q_1\to Q_0$ give the source and target of each arrow. Assume $Q$ has
no directed cycles. For a field $K$, a finite-dimensional representation $M$
assigns a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space $M_i$ to each $i\in Q_0$ and a
linear map $M_a:M_{s(a)}\to M_{t(a)}$ to each $a\in Q_1$. A morphism is a
family of linear maps at the vertices commuting with all arrow maps. Write
$\mathcal A_Q(K)$ for this category and
$\mathbf d(M)=(\dim_K M_i)_{i\in Q_0}\in\mathbb N^{Q_0}$ for its dimension
vector. For the finite-field Hall branch, fix $k=\mathbb F_q$ and write
$\mathcal A_Q=\mathcal A_Q(k)$. The next lemma proves the abelian and Euler
properties over any field, and the small finitary properties over $k$.

1. $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(M,N)$;
2. $\operatorname{YExt}^{1}_{\mathcal A}(M,N)$, the set of Yoneda classes of

   one-fold instance of the generated endpoint-fixed chain-map relation in

   $N$ and $M$, and the relation is closed under reflexivity, symmetry and

derivations.claim: For a morphism $f:X\to Y$, its vertexwise kernels form a subrepresentation: if $x\in\ker f_i$, then $f_jX_a(x)=Y_af_i(x)=0$ for every arrow $a:i\to j$. The vertexwise cokernels form a quotient representation because $Y_a(\operatorname{im}f_i)\subseteq\operatorname{im}f_j$. The kernel and cokernel universal properties hold vertex by vertex. The canonical coimage-to-image map is an isomorphism at every vertex, hence an isomorphism of representations. With vertexwise finite direct sums and a zero object, these facts make $\mathcal A_Q(K)$ abelian.

For $i\in Q_0$, let $P_i(v)$ have basis the directed paths from $i$ to $v$, with arrow maps given by path concatenation. Acyclicity and finiteness of $Q$ make each path set finite. A morphism $P_i\to N$ is uniquely determined by the image of the length-zero path at $i$, so $\operatorname{Hom}(P_i,N)\cong N_i$; evaluation at $i$ preserves epimorphisms, and therefore $P_i$ is projective.

Put $$C^0(X,Y)=\bigoplus_i\operatorname{Hom}_K(X_i,Y_i),\qquad C^1(X,Y)=\bigoplus_{a:i\to j}\operatorname{Hom}_K(X_i,Y_j),$$ and define $\partial:C^0\to C^1$ by $(\partial h)_a=Y_ah_i-h_jX_a$. Its kernel is exactly $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A_Q(K)}(X,Y)$ by the commuting-square definition of a representation morphism.

For a representation $X$, define $\epsilon:\bigoplus_iP_i\otimes_KX_i\to X$ by $p\otimes x\mapsto X_p(x)$, where $X_p$ is the composite arrow map along the path $p$. Define $$d:\bigoplus_{a:i\to j}P_j\otimes_KX_i\longrightarrow\bigoplus_iP_i\otimes_KX_i$$ at a path $p:j\to v$ by $$d(p\otimes x)=(p\otimes X_a(x))_j-((p\circ a)\otimes x)_i.$$ Both terms are finite direct sums of the projectives from step 1.2. Then $\epsilon d=0$ because $X_{p\circ a}=X_pX_a$.

Now assume $K=\mathbb F_q$. For each dimension vector $\mathbf d$, there are finitely many arrow matrix tuples on the fixed spaces $K^{d_i}$, and the finite group $G_{\mathbf d}(K)$ has finitely many orbits on this set. Fix an enumeration of the finite set $K$; the lexicographically least tuple in each orbit gives a representative without making a choice from an arbitrary family. The union over the set $\mathbb N^{Q_0}$ is a set, so the full subcategory on these representatives is small. It is a skeleton: every finite-dimensional representation becomes one of the matrix tuples after choosing bases at its finitely many vertices. The full skeleton is abelian because each vertexwise kernel and cokernel from step 1.1 is isomorphic to its selected representative, and transporting its kernel or cokernel map across that isomorphism preserves the universal property.

At vertex $v$, $\epsilon$ is onto because $x\in X_v$ is the image of $\operatorname{id}_v\otimes x$. Modulo $\operatorname{im}d$, the relation in step 2.1 replaces $(p\circ a)\otimes x$ by $p\otimes X_a(x)$. Every positive-length path has a unique first arrow, so repeated replacement sends each path tensor to $\operatorname{id}_v\otimes X_p(x)$. Consequently the quotient of the middle term by $\operatorname{im}d$ is isomorphic to $X_v$ through $\epsilon$, and $\ker\epsilon=\operatorname{im}d$.

The map $d$ is injective. In a nonzero element of its domain, choose the largest length $\ell$ of a suffix path $p$ with nonzero coefficient. The second term of $d(p\otimes x)$ has length $\ell+1$. Each such path has a unique first arrow and suffix, so its coefficient cannot cancel with the second term of a different source basis summand. A first term of $d$ has length at most $\ell$, since no source suffix has length $\ell+1$. Thus the length-$(\ell+1)$ part of $d$ is nonzero, proving injectivity. The displayed sequence is a projective resolution of length one; applying $\operatorname{Hom}(-,Y)$ therefore gives $\operatorname{Ext}^r_{\mathcal A_Q(K)}(X,Y)=0$ for $r\ge2$.

A short exact sequence $0\to Y\to E\to X\to0$ splits as a sequence of vector spaces at each of the finitely many vertices. In the resulting coordinates every arrow of $E$ has block matrix $$E_a=\begin{pmatrix}Y_a&\xi_a\\0&X_a\end{pmatrix},\qquad \xi_a\in\operatorname{Hom}_K(X_i,Y_j).$$ Every tuple $\xi\in C^1(X,Y)$ defines such an extension. Changing the vertexwise splittings by $h\in C^0(X,Y)$ changes $\xi$ by $\partial h$. Conversely, an isomorphism of extensions that is the identity on endpoints has block matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&h_i\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ at each vertex and hence changes $\xi$ by exactly $\partial h$. By [F3], the generated endpoint-fixed Yoneda relation consists of these isomorphisms. The Baer sum of the extensions represented by $\xi$ and $\eta$ is represented by $\xi+\eta$: the pullback of their direct sum along $X\to X\oplus X$ followed by pushout along $Y\oplus Y\to Y$ adds the off-diagonal arrow blocks. Pushout along $\lambda\operatorname{id}_Y$ sends $\xi$ to $\lambda\xi$. Therefore the Yoneda vector-space structure is the quotient structure $$\operatorname{YExt}^1(X,Y)\cong C^1(X,Y)/\operatorname{im}\partial,$$ a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space; it is not being identified here with the projective-resolution group of step 4.1.

Both cochain spaces in step 1.3 are finite-dimensional. Rank-nullity for $\partial$ gives $$\dim\ker\partial-\dim\operatorname{coker}\partial =\dim C^0-\dim C^1 =\sum_i d_i(X)d_i(Y)-\sum_{a:i\to j}d_i(X)d_j(Y) =\chi_Q(\mathbf d(X),\mathbf d(Y)).$$ The kernel and cokernel identifications already proved give the Hom–Yoneda-Ext$^1$ formula and finite-dimensionality over any $K$. When $K=\mathbb F_q$, the underlying sets are finite; together with the abelian and small-model arguments of steps 1.1 and 2.2, the category satisfies the small finitary abelian hypotheses of [F2].

These are zero-locus equations for bundle maps, so their common incidence locus $I_{\mathbf e}$ is closed. Its geometric points are exactly pairs consisting of an arrow matrix tuple and a subrepresentation of dimension $\mathbf e$.

By [A2] and [F2], every factor of $P_{\mathbf e}$ is a closed subvariety of a projective space. Iterating [F3] gives a closed projective embedding of their finite product into a projective space; if $Q_0$ is empty, the product is a point and is already projective. Thus the projection $\operatorname{Rep}_{\mathbf d}\times P_{\mathbf e}\to \operatorname{Rep}_{\mathbf d}$ is projective, and its restriction to the closed subvariety $I_{\mathbf e}$ is projective in the factorization sense of [F4].

By [A1] and [F5], the projection in step 1.2 is proper; [F6] then makes its image closed in $\operatorname{Rep}_{\mathbf d}(Q)_{\bar k}$. This image is exactly the locus of representations with a destabilizing subrepresentation of dimension $\mathbf e$.

Let $Q$ be a finite acyclic quiver and $K$ any field. The category
$\mathcal A_Q(K)$ of finite-dimensional representations is abelian. For all
$X,Y\in\mathcal A_Q(K)$, the spaces $\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)$ and Yoneda
$\operatorname{Ext}^1(X,Y)$ are finite-dimensional $K$-vector spaces, and
$$\dim_K\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)-\dim_K\operatorname{YExt}^1(X,Y) =\chi_Q(\mathbf d(X),\mathbf d(Y)).$$
The explicit projective resolution below shows that the projective-resolution
groups $\operatorname{Ext}^r_{\mathcal A_Q(K)}(X,Y)$ vanish for $r\ge2$; these
groups are the cohomology of applying $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A_Q(K)}(-,Y)$
to a projective resolution. If
$K=\mathbb F_q$, the displayed vector spaces have finite underlying sets and
$\mathcal A_Q(K)$ has a small skeleton (a small full subcategory with one
representative of each isomorphism class), so it is a small finitary abelian
category. Yoneda $\operatorname{Ext}^1$ is classified directly below; it is
not identified with derived $\operatorname{Ext}^1$ by an unstated theorem.

$\phi(z)=\arg(z)/\pi\in(0,1)$. For $z,w\in\mathbb H$, the phase of $z+w$

derivations.claim: Let $M\ne0$ have dimension vector $\mathbf d$. The nonzero dimension vectors of its subrepresentations form a nonempty subset of the finite set $\{\mathbf e:0\le e_i\le d_i\}$. Choose the largest attained phase and, among subobjects attaining it, the largest attained total dimension. Such a phase and dimension are maxima of finite sets of attained values, so they are attained without an infinite choice. Let $S\subseteq M$ attain both maxima. Every nonzero subobject of $S$ is a subobject of $M$, so its phase is at most $\phi_Z(S)$; hence $S$ is semistable.

If $A,B$ are semistable and $\phi_Z(A)>\phi_Z(B)$, then $\operatorname{Hom}(A,B)=0$. Indeed, a nonzero map has a nonzero image $I$. From $0\to\ker f\to A\to I\to0$, semistability of $A$ and [F3] force $\phi_Z(I)\ge\phi_Z(A)$: if the kernel is zero the phases are equal; if the kernel is nonzero and $\phi_Z(I)<\phi_Z(A)$, the phase of the sum lies strictly below $\phi_Z(A)$, contradicting $Z(A)=Z(\ker f)+Z(I)$. But $I\subseteq B$ and semistability of $B$ give $\phi_Z(I)\le\phi_Z(B)$, a contradiction.

If $T\subseteq M/S$ is nonzero, let $P\subseteq M$ be its inverse image. Then $0\to S\to P\to T\to0$ is exact. If $\phi_Z(T)>\phi_Z(S)$, [F3] gives $\phi_Z(P)>\phi_Z(S)$, contrary to maximality of the phase of $S$. If $\phi_Z(T)=\phi_Z(S)$, additivity and [F3] give $\phi_Z(P)=\phi_Z(S)$, while $|\mathbf d(P)|>|\mathbf d(S)|$, contrary to the second maximum. Thus every nonzero subobject of $M/S$ has phase strictly less than $\phi_Z(S)$.

Consider two filtrations with first subobjects $S,S'$ of phases $p,p'$. If $p>p'$, every factor in the quotient filtration of $M/S'$ has phase below $p'$. Step 1.2 therefore makes every map from $S$ to each such factor zero. Induction along the finite quotient filtration shows $\operatorname{Hom}(S,M/S')=0$: a map whose projection to the last factor is zero factors through the preceding subobject. Thus $S$ maps into $S'$, which contradicts semistability of $S'$ because $p>p'$. Interchanging $S,S'$ rules out $p'<p$ as well, so $p=p'$. Applying step 1.2 to all factors of both quotients now gives $S\subseteq S'$ and $S'\subseteq S$, hence $S=S'$. Induction on the quotient proves equality of the full filtrations.

Induct on $|\mathbf d(M)|$. The zero representation has the empty filtration. For $M\ne0$, the quotient $M/S$ has smaller total dimension, so by induction it has a filtration with semistable factors in strictly decreasing phase order. Step 2.1 places every one of those phases below $\phi_Z(S)$. Pulling that filtration back along $M\to M/S$ and placing $S$ first gives the required filtration of $M$.

Let $M$ be defined over $k$, set $M_{\bar k}=M\otimes_k\bar k$, and let $\sigma(x)=x^q$ be Frobenius. Applying $\sigma$ to a filtration preserves the arrow maps of $M_{\bar k}$, every dimension vector, and every phase. It therefore gives another HN filtration; uniqueness proved above fixes each term. At each vertex, a Frobenius-invariant subspace has a unique reduced row-echelon basis matrix. Applying $\sigma$ gives another such matrix for the same subspace, so uniqueness makes the matrix fixed entrywise. Its entries lie in $\mathbb F_q$, and the arrow maps of $M$ preserve these descended subspaces. Thus the filtration descends to $k$.

If an $\mathbb F_q$-object is geometrically unstable, it has a geometric subrepresentation of phase greater than its total phase. Step 1.1 chooses a subobject of maximal phase, so the first HN term has phase greater than the total phase. Step 4.1 descends that term and its phase inequality to $\mathbb F_q$, contradicting $\mathbb F_q$-semistability. Conversely, an $\mathbb F_q$-subrepresentation extends to $\bar k$ with the same dimension vector and phase. This proves the stated equivalence and the result.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for

derivations.claim: A representation is determined up to isomorphism by its dimension $n$; its automorphism group is $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$. For $n>0$, $Z(n)=nz_1$ and every nonzero subspace has the same phase, so every object is semistable. The zero object supplies the degree-zero term.

An ordered basis of $\mathbb F_q^n$ can be chosen in $$|\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)|= \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(q^n-q^j)$$ ways: after $j$ independent vectors have been chosen, their span contains $q^j$ vectors to exclude. Factoring $q^j$ from the $j$th term and reversing the remaining index gives $$|\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)|= q^{n(n-1)/2}\prod_{r=1}^{n}(q^r-1).$$ For $n=0$ both sides equal $1$.

The Euler form is $\chi_Q(n,n)=n^2$. By [F2], the degree-$n$ term of $J(A_{\mathrm{all}})$ is $$\frac{t^{n^2}}{|\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)|}x^n =\frac{t^n}{\prod_{r=1}^{n}(t^{2r}-1)}x^n,$$ using [F1], step 1.2 and $q=t^2$. The formula also holds at $n=0$ by the empty-product convention.

Summing the degreewise coefficients in step 2.1 gives the stated formal power series. By [F3] its unweighted coefficient is the finite groupoid cardinality of the semistable stack, and the factor $t^{n^2}$ is precisely the Euler normalization in [F2]. No physical state-counting identification is asserted.

derivations.claim: A representation is one linear map $f:V_1\to V_2$. Choose a complement to $\ker f$ and a complement to $\operatorname{im}f$. The restriction of $f$ from the first complement to $\operatorname{im}f$ is an isomorphism. In bases adapted to these spaces, the representation is $$S_1^{\oplus a}\oplus E^{\oplus r}\oplus S_2^{\oplus b},\qquad r=\operatorname{rank}f,\quad a=\dim\ker f,\quad b=\dim(V_2/\operatorname{im}f).$$ Thus these three isomorphism types account for every representation.

The Euler form gives $\chi_Q(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2)=-1$ and $\chi_Q(\mathbf e_2,\mathbf e_1)=0$, so $\langle\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2\rangle=-1$ and $\langle\mathbf e_2,\mathbf e_1\rangle=1$. By [F3], $$x_2*x_1=t\,x^{(1,1)},\qquad x_1*x_2=t^{-1}x^{(1,1)},\qquad x^{(1,1)}=t\,x_1*x_2.$$ In particular $x_2*x_1=t^2x_1*x_2$.

A subrepresentation of $E$ is a pair of subspaces $U_1,U_2\subseteq\mathbb F_q$ with $U_1\subseteq U_2$. Its only proper nonzero possibility is $S_2$. The phase of $z_1+z_2$ lies between $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ by [F4]. The sequence $0\to S_2\to E\to S_1\to0$ is nonsplit because $E$ has no subrepresentation isomorphic to $S_1$; every nonzero arrow scalar is changed to the identity by vertex base changes, so this is the unique nontrivial extension of these simples. Hence $E$ is stable when $\phi_1>\phi_2$, unstable when $\phi_1<\phi_2$, and strictly semistable when $\phi_1=\phi_2$.

Suppose $\phi_1>\phi_2$. In the decomposition of step 1.1, if two different summand types occur, the direct sum of all summands of greatest phase is a proper subobject. Repeated application of [F4] shows the total phase is strictly below that greatest phase, because at least one summand has smaller phase; hence the representation is unstable. Pure sums $S_1^{\oplus n}$ and $S_2^{\oplus n}$ are semistable because all their nonzero subobjects have the same phase. A subrepresentation of $E^{\oplus n}$ is a pair $U_1\subseteq U_2$; writing $r=\dim U_1$ and $s=\dim U_2$ gives $r\le s$. The determinant calculation $$\operatorname{Im}\big(\overline{(z_1+z_2)}(rz_1+sz_2)\big) =(s-r)\operatorname{Im}(\bar z_1z_2)\le0$$ shows its phase is at most that of $E^{\oplus n}$. Thus the semistable objects are exactly pure sums of $S_1$, $E$, or $S_2$, in descending phase order.

Suppose $\phi_1<\phi_2$. Every summand in the decomposition of step 1.1 has phase at most $\phi_2$, and an $E$ summand or an $S_1$ summand has smaller phase. Repeated application of [F4] therefore makes the phase of any object containing a lower-phase summand strictly less than $\phi_2$. An object with an $E$ summand has the nonzero subobject $S_2$, and an object with both $S_1$ and $S_2$ summands has an $S_2$ summand; each is a destabilizing subobject. Hence only pure sums of $S_2$ and pure sums of $S_1$ are semistable, in that descending order. If $\phi_1=\phi_2$, all nonzero dimension vectors have the same phase, so every representation is semistable and the HN product has one phase factor containing both $S_1\oplus S_2$ and $E$.

Each $A\in\{S_1,S_2,E\}$ has $\operatorname{End}(A)=\mathbb F_q$. For $E$, an endomorphism is a pair of scalars at the vertices that must agree because its arrow is the identity. Also $\chi_Q(\mathbf d(A),\mathbf d(A))=1$ for each of these three objects. [F5] gives $\operatorname{YExt}^1(A^{\oplus m},A^{\oplus n})=0$: the Hom space has dimension $mn$ and $\chi_Q(m\mathbf d(A),n\mathbf d(A))=mn$. The semistable subcategory at each stable phase in step 3.1 is consequently equivalent to $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathbb F_q}$, with the displayed object as its one-dimensional simple.

For $A$ one of these three stable objects, put $\gamma=\mathbf d(A)$. Then $\chi_Q(n\gamma,n\gamma)=n^2$ and $|\operatorname{Aut}(A^{\oplus n})|=|\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)|$. Counting ordered bases directly gives $$|\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)|= \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(q^n-q^j) =q^{n(n-1)/2}\prod_{r=1}^{n}(q^r-1).$$ Therefore $$\frac{t^{n^2}}{|\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)|} =\frac{t^n}{\prod_{r=1}^{n}(t^{2r}-1)}$$ using $q=t^2$. Thus the $J$-image of the semistable series at that phase is $E_{t^2}(x^\gamma)$. The empty product gives the same result for $n=0$.

If $\phi_1>\phi_2$, the descending semistable phases are $S_1,E,S_2$; if $\phi_1<\phi_2$, they are $S_2,S_1$. Apply [F2] to these two chamber assignments and substitute the phase images from steps 5.1 and 1.2. This gives the stated pentagon over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt q)$.

Each fixed-bidegree coefficient of the pentagon is a rational function of $t$. Specializing to $q=2^m$ for every $m\ge1$ gives infinitely many distinct $t=2^{m/2}>1$, where every denominator $t^{2r}-1$ is nonzero and step 6.1 proves equality. The numerator of the difference therefore has infinitely many roots and is the zero polynomial. This proves the identity coefficientwise in $\mathbb Q(t)$.
